checks.label: Verified Boot State
checks.description: Android Verified Boot state: green=fully verified, yellow=custom key, orange=unlocked, red=failed. Only green is production-safe.
checks.remediation: Re-lock bootloader and restore factory boot image to achieve green verified boot state.

checks.label: Build Tags (Release vs Test Keys)
checks.description: Build tags must be 'release-keys' for Play Integrity API basic integrity. 'test-keys' or 'dev-keys' will fail integrity checks.
checks.remediation: Use production/release-signed firmware. Test-key builds will fail Google Play Integrity checks.

checks.label: Samsung Knox Warranty Bit (ro.boot.warranty_bit)
checks.description: Samsung Knox warranty bit - '1' means Knox has been permanently tripped (OEM unlock occurred), disabling Knox security features.
checks.remediation: Knox warranty bit cannot be reset. Replace the device if Knox compliance is required.

checks.label: Samsung Knox Warranty Bit (ro.warranty_bit)
checks.description: Alternative Knox warranty bit property. Non-zero indicates Knox security has been permanently compromised.
checks.remediation: Knox warranty bit cannot be reset. Replace the device for Knox-required environments.

checks.label: Samsung Knox Version
checks.description: Samsung Knox version property. Indicates Knox is active and its version.
checks.remediation: Informational. Verify Knox version meets your compliance requirements.

checks.label: Samsung TIMA (TrustZone Integrity Measurement Architecture)
checks.description: Samsung TIMA provides TrustZone-based integrity measurement of the Linux kernel. Absence on Samsung devices may indicate Knox is not active.
checks.remediation: Informational. TIMA requires Knox-supported Samsung hardware and an active Knox license.

checks.label: Samsung RKP (Real-time Kernel Protection)
checks.description: Samsung RKP uses hypervisor technology to protect kernel integrity at runtime from TrustZone. A Samsung Knox security feature.
checks.remediation: Informational. RKP requires compatible Samsung Knox hardware.

checks.label: Titan M / Titan M2 Security Chip
checks.description: Google Titan M or Titan M2 dedicated security chip provides hardware-isolated key storage and verified boot anchoring (Pixel 3+).
checks.remediation: Informational. Titan M is only available on Pixel devices. Use StrongBox-backed keys for sensitive key material.

checks.label: Hardware Security Level (StrongBox)
checks.description: Hardware security level property. 'StrongBox' indicates dedicated security chip (Titan M/M2 or equivalent).
checks.remediation: Informational. For highest security, prefer devices with StrongBox-level hardware security.

checks.label: Google Play Protect (Package Verifier)
checks.description: Google Play Protect package verifier must be enabled for malware scanning. Disabled state bypasses Play Integrity checks.
checks.remediation: Enable Play Protect: adb shell settings put global package_verifier_enable 1

checks.label: Play Protect ADB Install Verification
checks.description: Play Protect should verify apps installed via ADB. Disabled allows unverified sideloads to bypass integrity checks.
checks.remediation: Enable ADB install verification: adb shell settings put global verifier_verify_adb_installs 1

checks.label: MagiskHide / DenyList Active
checks.description: Magisk Hide active - root is being concealed from SafetyNet/Play Integrity checks. Device is rooted but hiding it.
checks.remediation: Device is rooted and actively bypassing integrity checks. Remove Magisk and restore the stock boot image.

checks.label: SafetyNet / Play Integrity Bypass Modules
checks.description: SafetyNet/Play Integrity bypass modules (Shamiko, Universal SafetyNet Fix, etc.) found in Magisk modules directory.
checks.remediation: Remove bypass modules and Magisk. These modules actively tamper with integrity attestation.

checks.label: APK Verity Mode (fs-verity for APKs)
checks.command: V=$(getprop ro.apk_verity.mode 2>/dev/null); [ -z "$V" ] && echo "UNMEASURED ro.apk_verity.mode unset" || printf '%s\n' "$V"
checks.description: APK verity mode 2 = fs-verity enforced for APKs (Android 12+). Mode 0 or 1 means no or partial APK integrity verification.
checks.remediation: Ensure device runs Android 12+ with official firmware. APK verity requires fs-verity kernel support.

checks.label: fs-verity Kernel Support
checks.command: if [ -d /sys/fs/verity ] || [ -e /sys/fs/verity/require_signatures ]; then S=$(cat /sys/fs/verity/require_signatures 2>/dev/null); echo "FSVERITY_SYSFS_PRESENT require_signatures=${S:-unset}"; else M=$(getprop ro.apk_verity.mode 2>/dev/null); echo "FSVERITY_SYSFS_ABSENT apk_verity_mode=${M:-unset}"; fi
checks.description: fs-verity provides transparent, read-time integrity verification of individual files using a Merkle tree, and Android uses it from API 30 to protect installed APKs and select system files. Support is visible through the /sys/fs/verity directory, and Android's own usage level through the ro.apk_verity.mode property (0 disabled, 1 enabled, 2 enforced). This replaces an earlier version that read /proc/sys/fs/verity, a path that does not exist on Android, and then silently fell back to printing ro.product.first_api_level under an fs-verity label with a safe_pattern of '.' that could never fail.
checks.remediation: Set ro.apk_verity.mode to 2 to enforce APK fs-verity, and confirm the kernel is built with CONFIG_FS_VERITY=y and the userdata filesystem has the verity feature enabled.

checks.label: Android Enterprise Work Profile
checks.command: dumpsys device_policy 2>/dev/null | grep -i -E 'enabled profiles|managed profile' | head -3
checks.description: Android Enterprise work profiles indicate managed device with MDM attestation controls active.
checks.remediation: Informational. Verify work profile policies meet your compliance requirements.

checks.label: First API Level (Attestation Baseline)
checks.description: First API level shipped determines hardware attestation baseline. API 28+ = key attestation, API 32+ = Play Integrity API support.
checks.remediation: Informational. Devices shipping with Android 9+ (API 28) support hardware-backed key attestation.

checks.label: Knox DualDAR Encryption Status
checks.description: Samsung Knox DualDAR provides dual-layer encryption: AOSP FBE (Android layer) + Knox MDM-controlled second layer.
checks.remediation: Informational. DualDAR requires Knox license and MDM enrollment.

checks.label: Hardware-Backed Keystore / KeyMint HAL Present
checks.command: F=$(pm list features 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'hardware_keystore|strongbox' | tr '\n' ' '); H=$(getprop ro.hardware.keystore 2>/dev/null); L=$(lshal 2>/dev/null | grep -oiE 'keymint@[0-9.]+|keymaster@[0-9.]+' | sort -u | tr '\n' ' '); echo "features=${F:-none} hal_prop=${H:-unset} hal=${L:-unavailable}"
checks.description: Hardware key attestation is the root of every attestation claim this category makes. It requires a KeyMint (Android 12+) or Keymaster (older) HAL backing the keystore. The android.hardware.hardware_keystore feature is reported with a version suffix (for example =300 for KeyMint 3.0) and android.hardware.strongbox_keystore indicates a discrete secure element. If none of these are present, the device has no hardware-backed key storage: keys live in software, attestation certificates cannot be chained to a Google-signed root, and the other ATTESTATION checks describe policy rather than enforced hardware. The lshal probe is best-effort because non-root shells on some user builds cannot enumerate HALs, so 'hal=unavailable' alone is not a failure.
checks.remediation: Hardware-backed keystore cannot be added in software. If this fails on production hardware, confirm the keystore HAL is declared in the device manifest and the SoC vendor shipped a KeyMint implementation. Do not rely on key attestation, StrongBox, or Play Integrity hardware verdicts on a device without it.
checks.why: Every hardware attestation claim, StrongBox key, and device-integrity verdict chains back to a KeyMint or Keymaster HAL. Without one the chain has no hardware root.
checks.risk_if_fail: Cryptographic keys are software-only and extractable from a rooted or compromised device, and attestation certificates cannot prove the device state.

checks.label: Remote Key Provisioning (Attestation Key Certification)
checks.command: P=$(pm list packages 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'rkpdapp|remoteprovisioner' | sed 's/^package://' | tr '\n' ' '); L=$(lshal 2>/dev/null | grep -oiE 'IRemotelyProvisionedComponent[^ ]*' | sort -u | head -3 | tr '\n' ' '); echo "rkp_app=${P:-none} rkp_hal=${L:-unavailable}"
checks.description: Remote Key Provisioning replaced factory-installed attestation key batches on Android 12 and later: the device generates keys locally and has them certified on demand by a Google backend, so a leaked factory key batch can be revoked without bricking attestation. Not to be confused with Samsung RKP (Real-time Kernel Protection), which is a separate check in this category. This reports whether the provisioning daemon app and the IRemotelyProvisionedComponent HAL are present. Informational rather than pass or fail: remote provisioning is part of the GMS ecosystem, so AOSP builds, non-GMS OEM builds, and many POS or industrial devices legitimately have neither, and their absence is a deployment fact to record rather than a misconfiguration.
checks.remediation: Nothing to fix directly. Record the result as part of the attestation baseline. If the deployment depends on revocable attestation keys, confirm with the OEM that the device participates in RKP rather than shipping a static factory key batch.

checks.label: TrickyStore Attestation Spoofing Framework
checks.description: TrickyStore hooks the Android Keystore layer and injects a third-party attestation key (a leaked 'keybox') into the certificate chain returned by getCertificateChain(). The result is a chain that a backend validates as genuine while the underlying device is rooted with an unlocked bootloader. This inverts the usual root-detection problem: every other root artifact makes a device look broken, this one makes a compromised device look healthy. Presence of the module directory or its config directory is direct evidence that hardware key attestation output from this device cannot be trusted.
checks.remediation: Remove the module with 'rm -rf /data/adb/modules/tricky_store /data/adb/tricky_store' and reboot, then delete any keybox material found by ATT-024. Treat every attestation this device produced while the module was installed as forged. On a fleet device, reflash stock firmware and relock the bootloader.
checks.why: It forges a valid-looking hardware attestation chain, so a backend cannot tell this device from a locked, verified one.
checks.risk_if_fail: Any service relying on key attestation from this device has been given a fabricated device-integrity verdict.

checks.label: Attestation Keybox Key Material On Disk
checks.description: A keybox.xml holds an attestation private key and its certificate chain, normally sealed inside the TEE or StrongBox and never exposed to the filesystem. A copy sitting on disk is leaked or extracted key material, and it is what attestation-spoofing tooling loads to sign forged chains. This is the failure mode the Google attestation revocation list exists to contain: factory-provisioned batch keys cover many devices, so one leaked keybox lets every device in that batch be impersonated until the key is revoked. Detected independently of TrickyStore because the file is a finding regardless of which tool placed it.
checks.remediation: Delete the file and reboot. Report the keybox to the device vendor or to Google so the key can be added to the attestation status list at https://android.googleapis.com/attestation/status. Do not accept attestation from this device until it is reflashed.
checks.why: An attestation private key outside secure hardware can sign arbitrary forged attestation chains.
checks.risk_if_fail: Attestation chains from this device, and potentially from every device sharing the same factory batch key, can be fabricated.

checks.label: TrickyStore Spoofing Target Configuration
checks.description: TrickyStore reads target.txt to decide which application packages receive a forged attestation chain, and security_patch.txt to decide which security patch level to report back instead of the real one. Where ATT-023 proves the framework is installed, this check extracts the operator's intent: the exact list of apps being lied to and the fake patch level being advertised. On an incident response engagement this is the most directly useful artifact of the three, because it names the targeted services.
checks.remediation: Preserve both files as evidence before deletion. Notify every service listed in target.txt that attestation and security patch level from this device were forged, then remove the module per ATT-023.
checks.why: The target list names which services were given a forged device-integrity verdict, and the patch file names the fake security patch level advertised to them.
checks.risk_if_fail: Named services accepted a fabricated attestation and a fabricated security patch level from a rooted device.

checks.label: Replay Protected Memory Block (RPMB) Availability
checks.command: R=$(ls -d /dev/block/mmcblk0rpmb /dev/block/by-name/rpmb /dev/block/sda* 2>/dev/null | grep -i rpmb | tr '\n' ' '); S=$(ls /sys/block/mmcblk0rpmb 2>/dev/null | head -1); [ -z "$R" ] && [ -z "$S" ] && echo RPMB_NOT_VISIBLE || echo "RPMB_PRESENT nodes=${R:-none} sysfs=${S:-none}"
checks.description: Reports whether a Replay Protected Memory Block partition is visible. RPMB is the authenticated, replay-resistant storage that the TEE uses for rollback counters, Keymaster and KeyMint key metadata, and Gatekeeper failed-attempt counters. Without it, the counters that enforce lockout after failed unlock attempts and that prevent rollback of encrypted state have no tamper-resistant home. RPMB_NOT_VISIBLE is common and not itself a finding: on many devices the block is claimed by the secure world and never exposed to the Linux side, which is the stronger configuration. Informational for that reason.
checks.remediation: Nothing to act on directly. Confirm with the SoC vendor that RPMB is provisioned and that Gatekeeper and KeyMint use it for counter storage, since lockout enforcement and rollback resistance depend on it.

checks.label: OTA Update Signing Certificates
checks.command:
F=$(ls /system/etc/security/otacerts.zip /vendor/etc/security/otacerts.zip 2>/dev/null | head -2 | tr '
' ' '); if [ -z "$F" ]; then echo NO_OTACERTS; else T=$(grep -al 'android@android.com' $F /system/etc/security/*.x509.pem 2>/dev/null | head -2 | tr '
' ' '); H=$(sha256sum $F 2>/dev/null | awk '{print substr($1,1,16)}' | tr '
' ' '); [ -n "$T" ] && echo "AOSP_TESTKEY_PRESENT in=$T" || echo "OTACERTS_PRESENT sha256_prefix=${H:-unknown}"; fi
checks.description: Reports the OTA update signing certificate bundle and searches it for the AOSP test key. Android verifies update packages against the certificates in otacerts.zip, so a device shipping the public AOSP test key accepts any OTA an attacker can sign with a key everybody has, which is full persistent compromise delivered through the normal update path. Detection greps for the android@android.com subject that the AOSP testkey carries. This is best effort: if the zip stores the certificate deflated rather than stored, the string will not match, so a clean result is not proof the testkey is absent. The certificate hash is reported and carries a baseline_key so a change to the OTA trust anchor is caught by --baseline. Companion to the existing Build Tags check, which reads ro.build.tags rather than the certificates themselves.
checks.remediation: Reflash with an image signed by production release keys and confirm otacerts.zip contains only the vendor's own OTA certificate. Never ship a device whose OTA trust anchor is the AOSP test key.
checks.why: An OTA trust anchor set to a publicly available key lets anyone sign an update the device will install.
checks.risk_if_fail: Persistent full-system compromise delivered through the normal update mechanism.

checks.label: Secure Boot Fuse and Provisioning State
checks.command: S=$(getprop ro.boot.secureboot 2>/dev/null); F=$(getprop ro.boot.fuse.secure 2>/dev/null); H=$(getprop ro.boot.hwc 2>/dev/null); D=$(getprop ro.boot.hw.revision 2>/dev/null); E=$(getprop ro.boot.enable_dm_verity 2>/dev/null); echo "secureboot=${S:-unset} secure_fuse=${F:-unset} hwc=${H:-unset} hw_rev=${D:-unset} dm_verity=${E:-unset}"
checks.description: Reports the boot properties that OEMs use to expose secure boot fuse and hardware provisioning state. On a production device the secure boot fuse is blown, permanently binding the boot ROM to the vendor's root key, and an unblown fuse means the entire chain of trust that Verified Boot and key attestation rest on can be bypassed by flashing an unsigned bootloader. Property names are entirely OEM-specific and many vendors expose none of this to Linux, so this is a best-effort evidence collector reported for review rather than a pass or fail. Definitive fuse state requires vendor tooling or hardware inspection and cannot be established from a shell.
checks.remediation: Confirm with the SoC vendor that the secure boot fuse is blown on production units and that engineering samples with unblown fuses are tracked and never shipped. Treat any device where this cannot be established as untrusted for attestation purposes.
